clue.text: Rude nature of open elitism developing over son

indicators.note: Something developing is changing shape as it grows, so the letters it points at need not stay in the order they were given.
In a down entry the thing said to be over another is written above it, so the shuffled letters sit on top of the letter below.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
s is the standard short form for son

explanation.surface: Class snobbery out in the open, deepening as it is handed down to a son.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' is a real instruction rather than scenery: it sends the son's letter to the foot of the column. 'Developing' is the gentlest sort of anagram signal, reading in the surface as ordinary growth.
explanation.definitionFit: Impoliteness is the abstract quality of being rude, so 'Rude nature' asks for the noun naming the trait rather than for a rude person.

clue.text: Institution treated hips a lot?

indicators.note: A patient who is treated is worked on and comes out altered, and so do the letters the word points at.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A great many hip complaints being seen to.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is drawn from the answer's own world, which is what makes it invisible: hips are exactly what the place in the definition treats. 'A lot' is fodder rather than a measure of quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospital is an institution in the formal sense — an established body with staff, buildings and a public duty — not merely a building.

clue.text: Footwear was highly polished but not new

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes whatever it names, so that letter is struck out of the word standing before it.

parts.note: something buffed to a high polish shone
n is the standard short form for new, and that is the letter to come out

explanation.surface: Footwear that gleamed although it was not new.
explanation.walkthrough: The tense is the key: 'was highly polished' wants the past verb, not the adjective shiny, and only the verb carries the letter that goes. The definition is the single word at the front, standing quietly apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe is the commonest single article of footwear, so the general word names the particular thing by category.

clue.text: Badger lashes out

indicators.note: Something that has come out is no longer in its place, so the letters in front of the word are loose and can be reset.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A cornered badger striking out at whatever comes near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' is the animal in the picture and a verb in the parse — to badger someone is to keep on at them. A three-word clue gives you almost nothing to grip, so the definition has to be one of the two ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To hassle someone is to pester them without let-up, the same persistent harrying that 'badger' names as a verb.

clue.text: Manage cutting mostly superior colour of hair

definitions.note: Strictly a brunette is the woman rather than the shade, but the word has long been used of the colour itself — 'she dyed it brunette' — and that is the sense the definition takes.

indicators.note: 'Mostly' asks for most of a word and not the whole of it, which means letting its final letter go.
To cut into a thing is to go inside it, so the word in front is planted within the word that follows.

parts.note: better means superior, docked of its last letter
to run a business is to manage it

explanation.surface: Coping with cutting hair of a mostly superior shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superior' looks like an adjective describing the colour and is really the comparative better, shaved of its tail. All the talk of cutting keeps you thinking about scissors rather than about one word going inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunette is the word for dark brown hair, borrowed from the French feminine, and it is used of the shade as readily as of the woman wearing it.

clue.text: Fashionable bird Kenneth's abandoned

indicators.note: What has been abandoned is gone, so the letters it names are taken out of the word before it.

parts.note: the farmyard bird, spelt out in full
Ken is the everyday short form of Kenneth, and those three letters are the ones to go

explanation.surface: A stylish girl whom Kenneth has walked out on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is dated British slang for a young woman, which is the reading the surface wants; the parse needs the farmyard sense instead. Setters shorten first names on sight, so Kenneth arriving as Ken is standard practice rather than a liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic means stylish in a sleek, understated, French way, so it stands in for 'fashionable' as an adjective describing a person or a look.

clue.text: Loiter in low church

parts.note: to low is what cattle do, and the noise they make is spelt this way
ch is the standard short form for church

explanation.surface: Hanging about at the back of a Low Church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' is the cattle verb here, not the adjective the sentence offers. Low Church is a genuine strand of Anglicanism, plain in its worship, which is why the two words read as one thing rather than as two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To mooch is to drift about with nothing much to do, the aimless hanging around that 'loiter' names.

clue.text: Broadcasts with cool craft

parts.note: a station airs a programme when it broadcasts it
hip means fashionably in the know, which is one sense of cool

explanation.surface: Programmes going out with a certain effortless style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' is the trap: it reads as skill in a sentence about broadcasting and means a vessel in the parse, the same sense that sits inside aircraft and hovercraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Craft is the collective word for a vessel that travels, by water or by air, and it covers a lighter-than-air ship exactly.

clue.text: Defend what Speaker does for country under another government

parts.note: to protect something is to defend it
to orate is to make a formal speech, which is a speaker's job

explanation.surface: A defence of what the Speaker of the House does on behalf of a dependency.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Speaker' points at the Commons official and is there for the surface alone; any speaker at all serves the wordplay. The definition is the whole back half of the clue, long enough to pass for scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A protectorate is a state whose defence and foreign affairs are run by a stronger power, so the clue's long phrase is a plain description of one.

clue.text: Hold down work with part of the media

parts.note: op is short for opus, a composer's work
the press is the newspaper arm of the media

explanation.surface: Holding down a job at a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold down' reads as the idiom for keeping a job, which is what lets the sentence hang together; as a definition it is the harsher political sense. Op for work comes off concert programmes and is one of the oldest shorthands going.
explanation.definitionFit: To oppress a people is to hold them down, keeping them subdued by weight of power — the same transitive verb the phrase gives.

clue.text: A portion of spinach or maize snack

indicators.note: A portion is a piece taken from something larger, so what is wanted is a run of letters lifted straight out of the words that follow.

parts.note: five letters in a row here, straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A helping of spinach, or else something made of corn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' is load-bearing: it belongs inside the concealed run rather than offering the choice the sentence pretends to. Both foods named are plausible in a clue about eating, so nothing looks out of place.
explanation.definitionFit: A nacho is a tortilla chip, and tortillas are made from maize, so 'maize snack' names it by material and by the way it is eaten.

clue.text: Quiet — new time traveller is breaking it

definitions.note: 'Quiet' is an adjective while the solution is usually a noun, but dictionaries list it as an adjective too, meaning inward-turned and reserved, and that is the sense the setter takes.

indicators.note: To break into something is to force a way inside it, so the letters assembled beforehand are driven into the middle of the word named next.

parts.note: the clue's own word, taken literally and split so the rest lands between its two letters
n is the standard short form for new
t is the standard short form for time
a rover is someone who wanders from place to place

explanation.surface: A time traveller from the new series bursting in on something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is the hardest word to see, because a pronoun feels like grammar rather than material — here it is the container the rest is shoved into. 'New time traveller' reads as one phrase and is three separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An introvert draws energy from their own company and says little in a crowd, which is what calling someone quiet means in everyday use.

clue.text: One tried moving to get lined up

indicators.note: Things that are moving are no longer where they were, so the letters shift out of the order the clue gives them.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Somebody who had a go at moving house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' does two jobs at once: in the sentence it is the thing attempted, in the parse it is the instruction. 'Lined up' is the physical sense of facing a set direction, not the sense of forming a queue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something oriented has been set facing a particular way, which is what 'lined up' says when it means aligned rather than queued.

clue.text: Odd characters in crude signal

indicators.note: Odd counts positions here rather than describing anyone, so the first, third and fifth letters of the word that follows are the ones taken.

parts.note: the letters standing in the odd positions, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: Strange people mixed up in a vulgar gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means letters, and 'odd' counts them instead of describing them — between them they make one of the tidiest ways of asking for alternate letters. The definition is a single word at the end, easy to lose in a clue this short.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is the signal that tells an actor when to speak or move, so the everyday word names the theatrical thing.

clue.text: Horse box enthusiast

parts.note: a chest is a stout box for storing things
someone described as a nut about something is an enthusiast for it

explanation.surface: Somebody mad keen on horseboxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horsebox' is a real compound, which is why three words look like two and the definition looks like half a noun. Colour words standing in for the animal itself — bay, grey, roan — are ordinary stable talk and reliable crossword material.
explanation.definitionFit: A chestnut is a horse of a reddish-brown colour, so 'Horse' defines it by kind: in the stable the coat names the animal.

clue.text: Gently handle headless fish that's slippery

indicators.note: Something headless has lost its front, so the opening letter of the word before it comes away.

parts.note: to feel something is to handle it gently

explanation.surface: Take care picking up a slippery fish with its head off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headless' belongs to the wordplay rather than to the fish, though the sentence hands you a decapitated one to picture. Four words of definition for three letters of answer is generous, and 'slippery' is doing honest work in both readings.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a long snake-like fish whose skin is coated in mucus, so 'slippery' is literally true of it as well as being its figurative reputation.

clue.text: Fellows interrupting devil allowed to execute

parts.note: an imp is a small mischievous devil

indicators.note: To interrupt is to cut in part-way through, so the letters named first are planted inside the word they break into.

parts.note: to let someone do a thing is to allow it
fellows is an old-fashioned word for men

explanation.surface: Some men cutting across a devil who has been given leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allowed' has to be heard as the bare verb let before it will split in two, and the past-tense ending hides that. 'Execute' is meant in its administrative sense, carrying a plan out, with nothing in the sentence steering you away from the other one.
explanation.definitionFit: To implement a policy is to carry it out in practice, which is what 'execute' means in its official sense rather than its capital-punishment one.

clue.text: Person giving many a tap salesman's spiel

definitions.meaning: an agent noun coined on the spot from the verb to pat
the fast practised talk used to keep a customer listening

explanation.surface: Someone reeling off the sales talk of a man who sells taps.
explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions run together with no join at all, so 'tap salesman' reads as a single occupation. The first is an agent noun built on the spot from the verb to pat — a setter may coin one, and a dictionary need not carry it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pats, over and over, is a patter; and patter is also the fast practised talk a salesman reels off to keep a customer listening.

clue.text: Taken in and defeated, losing billions

indicators.note: What is lost is gone for good, so the letter named after this word is dropped out of the word before it.

parts.note: a defeated side has been beaten
b is the standard short form for billions, and that letter is the one to go

explanation.surface: An investor duped, beaten and billions out of pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' means duped in the sentence and swallowed in the definition — fraud on the surface, food underneath. Setters treat the plural billions as worth the same single letter as billion, which is worth knowing before you hunt for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been eaten has been taken into the body, the literal sense of the phrase that the surface's swindling sense conceals.

clue.text: Fighting vehicle to fail disastrously

definitions.meaning: the armoured tracked machine of modern warfare
the verb for collapsing utterly, said of films and share prices

explanation.surface: A headline warning that an armoured vehicle is about to flop.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is American in origin and now everywhere — a film does it at the box office, a share price does it overnight. Two definitions with a link word between them is the standard shape, and the shortest clues are where it hides best.
explanation.definitionFit: A tank is the armoured tracked vehicle of modern warfare; and to tank is to collapse utterly, as a film does when nobody comes.

clue.text: What's driven thespian to chase leading parts in The Rivals

indicators.note: To chase someone is to come along behind them, so the thespian's letters are written after the ones already found.
The leading part of a word is its front, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is taken.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the two words
a thespian is an actor by trade

explanation.surface: An actor going after the lead roles in Sheridan's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rivals is Sheridan's 1775 comedy, so 'leading parts' is precisely what an actor would chase in it — theatre talk that is quietly asking for initials. 'What's driven' reads as a question about motive rather than about machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: 'What's driven' asks for a thing that gets driven, and a tractor is the farm machine with a driver sitting on top of it.

clue.text: What begins attaching leather sole on to boot

indicators.note: What begins a word is its first letter, so each word that follows gives up only its opening character.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words in turn

explanation.surface: A cobbler fixing a leather sole onto a boot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To boot' is an old idiom meaning in addition, and a sentence about footwear is the perfect place to hide it. 'On' is fodder rather than a joiner: the initials need four words and the clue supplies exactly four.
explanation.definitionFit: 'To boot' means as well or in addition, nothing to do with footwear, and 'also' is the plain adverb that would replace it.

clue.text: Not hypocritical after religious education

parts.note: since means from a given time onwards, as in 'nothing since Tuesday'
RE is the British school subject, religious education on a timetable

explanation.surface: Someone who stopped being a hypocrite after taking religious education.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like the joint between definition and wordplay and is in fact the first chunk of the wordplay itself. RE is a timetable subject in British schools, abbreviated the same way on every report, and reliably worth two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sincere person means what they say, so 'Not hypocritical' defines by ruling out the opposite rather than by offering a synonym.

clue.text: Short and wide building occupied illegally

definitions.meaning: the adjective for something low and thick-set
the noun for a house lived in without the owner's leave

explanation.surface: A low broad building that has been taken over by people with no right to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions run straight into one another with no join, so the sentence reads as a single description of one building. The second is British in flavour: a house lived in without the owner's leave has had its own one-word name since the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means short and thick-set, too broad for its height; as a noun, a building lived in with no legal right.
